title: The kings of Judah and Queen Athaliah

intro.text: Twenty rulers sat on the throne in Jerusalem from the division of the kingdom to the exile: nineteen kings of David's line and Queen Athaliah. These pages count her, so Hezekiah is the thirteenth ruler and Zedekiah the twentieth.
Kings names the mother of seventeen of the nineteen kings; it leaves out Jehoram's and Ahaz's. Chronicles names nine in its formula, from Rehoboam to Hezekiah, and none after him.

Kings says eight kings of Judah did "right": Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joash, Amaziah, Azariah, Jotham, Hezekiah and Josiah. For the first six it adds that the high places were not removed; Hezekiah removed them and Josiah defiled them.
Kings and 2 Chronicles tell these reigns twice. Each page shows the two records side by side and lists where they differ, without merging them.

Where Chronicles and Kings disagree, some prefer Kings as the older work unless its text is corrupt (Jewish Encyclopedia, 1903); others hold that Kings' silence about matters concerning Judah alone "is normal" and is no evidence against Chronicles (W. E. Barnes, 1899). This page shows both books and does not choose.

Dates are reconstructions. The main dates shown are Thiele's system as revised by McFall (1991): Rehoboam from 931/930 BC, Jerusalem's fall in 586. Young (2005) moves Rehoboam one year earlier and the fall to 587; Albright (1945) puts the division about 922; Ussher's traditional dates (1658) put it at 975. Thiele first published his system in 1944.

rulers.name: Rehoboam
rulers.title: King of Judah
rulers.tagline: Seventeen years in Jerusalem, as the kingdom split in two.

identifications.text: Shishak of the Bible is identified with Shoshenq I of Egypt's 22nd dynasty. Champollion, who read the Karnak relief in 1828, wrote that the identity he had already proposed was confirmed there; Breasted (1906) dates the campaign to Rehoboam's fifth year. A minority of revisionist writers reject the identification.

reign.text: Seventeen years, from the age of forty-one (1 Kgs 14:21; 2 Chr 12:13).

dates.note: 17 years (1 Kgs 14:21). Scripture gives lengths and cross-dates, never BC years.

verdictNotes.text: Kings gives Rehoboam no verdict of his own. It says Judah did evil in his reign, building high places and images, with "sodomites in the land".
Chronicles says he and Judah walked in the way of David and Solomon for three years, then forsook the law once the kingdom was strong.
Chronicles alone tells that the king and princes humbled themselves when Shemaiah spoke, so the LORD did not destroy them altogether, "and also in Judah things went well".

accession.text: He went to Shechem to be made king over all Israel. The people asked him to lighten Solomon's heavy yoke; he refused on the young men's advice, and the ten northern tribes rejected the house of David.
Kings says the outcome was "from the LORD", to fulfil Ahijah's word to Jeroboam.
Only the tribe of Judah followed the house of David; Benjamin is counted with Judah when Rehoboam musters his army.

claim.text: Rehoboam answered the people roughly; Israel said "What portion have we in David?" and went home. His tribute officer Adoram was stoned and he fled to Jerusalem.
He gathered 180,000 men of Judah and Benjamin to fight Israel, but Shemaiah brought the word "Ye shall not go up", and they went home.
He built fifteen cities for defence in Judah and Benjamin, from Bethlehem to Hebron, and stocked them with food, shields and spears.
Priests and Levites cast off by Jeroboam left their lands in the north and came to Judah, strengthening the kingdom for three years.
In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt came against Jerusalem and took the treasures of the temple and the palace, and Solomon's gold shields.
He made shields of brass in place of the gold ones, kept in the guard chamber.

events.label: War with Jeroboam all his days

claim.text: There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days.
Chronicles counts eighteen wives, sixty concubines, twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters; he loved Maachah daughter of Absalom most and made her son Abijah chief among his brothers.

worship.text: Judah built high places, images and groves "on every high hill, and under every green tree".
Chronicles: Levites and those who sought the LORD came to Jerusalem from all Israel to sacrifice.

building.text: Fifteen fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin (Chronicles).
Brass shields to replace the gold ones Shishak took.

alliances.text: No alliance is recorded. Egypt came as an invader; Chronicles says Judah would serve Shishak so as to know "the service of the kingdoms of the countries".

people.text: Israel rebelled against the house of David "unto this day"; only those who lived in the cities of Judah stayed under Rehoboam.
Shishak brought chariots, horsemen and Lubims, Sukkiims and Ethiopians, and took the fenced cities of Judah (Chronicles).

claim.text: The man of God who stopped Rehoboam's war against Israel, and later told him Judah was left in Shishak's hand because they had forsaken the LORD.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.

claim.text: His earlier word to Jeroboam, that ten tribes would be torn from Solomon's son, is named as the reason Rehoboam would not listen.
Chronicles names "Iddo the seer concerning genealogies" with Shemaiah as a written source for Rehoboam's acts.
Shishak, who had sheltered Jeroboam, invaded Judah in Rehoboam's fifth year.

A relief on the south wall of Amun's temple at Karnak shows Pharaoh Shoshenq I presenting rows of captives, each body a ring holding a town's name: 156 in all, of which about 75 can be read, in two groups Breasted took as towns of Israel and of Judah (Megiddo, Taanach, Gibeon, Beth-horon, Aijalon, Socoh, Arad and others).

outside.name: What the Karnak list does not say

claim.text: No king of Judah is named and Jerusalem is not among the names that can still be read ("We look in vain for Jerusalem", Breasted wrote). Many rings are lost, so the absence settles nothing either way. A ring once read as "king of Judah" is a place-name.

first.text: Kings gives the invasion in four verses: Shishak came and took the treasures and the gold shields.

second.text: Chronicles adds the army's size and peoples, the taking of Judah's fenced cities, Shemaiah's message, the king's humbling and the LORD's partial relief.

first.text: Kings speaks of what Judah did in his reign: "Judah did evil".

second.text: Chronicles speaks of the king himself: "he did evil, because he prepared not his heart to seek the LORD".

first.text: Kings has nothing of his building, the Levites' move south, or his family.

second.text: Chronicles tells all three.

questions.question: Did Shishak take Jerusalem itself?

argument.text: Shishak plundered the treasures of the temple and the palace, so he must have captured the city.
Jerusalem surrendered, but was preserved from destruction when the people repented at Shemaiah's call.
Shishak was bought off with a heavy present, as Sennacherib later was by Hezekiah.

questions.question: Why does Chronicles tell Shishak's invasion so much more fully?

argument.text: Keil reads Chronicles as a fuller account of the same expedition and notes that the Karnak list confirms it.

views.label: It is the Chronicler's reading of history
views.holders: W. E. Barnes (1899); C. J. Ellicott's commentary

argument.text: "Because they had transgressed" is the Chronicler's own explanation; he sees temporal reward and punishment at work everywhere. Barnes adds that the Chronicler may be wrong in linking a sin to a calamity while both facts are true.

notSaid: Scripture does not say why Rehoboam's mother, an Ammonite, is named twice in Kings (1 Kgs 14:21, 31); it simply repeats it.
Scripture does not say Shishak captured Jerusalem itself; both books say he "came up against Jerusalem" and took its treasures.
Kings and Chronicles give no year for his building work or for the three faithful years.

Chronicles gives no verdict. It tells instead of his speech to Israel on Mount Zemaraim and a victory won "because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers".

quote.text: Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam the son of Nebat reigned Abijam over Judah.
Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam began Abijah to reign over Judah.

claim.text: Rehoboam made Abijah, son of his favourite wife Maachah, chief among his brothers, meaning to make him king.
Before the battle he called on Jeroboam and Israel to remember the LORD's covenant of salt with David, and said Judah kept the priests and the temple service.
Caught between an ambush and the front line, Judah cried to the LORD; God smote Israel, and Chronicles says 500,000 of Israel fell.
He pursued Jeroboam and took Bethel, Jeshanah and Ephrain with their towns.
Kings says only that there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.
He married fourteen wives and had twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.

worship.text: Kings: he walked in his father's sins.
Chronicles: in his speech he says Judah kept the priests, the sons of Aaron, the daily offerings, the shewbread and the lamps.

alliances.text: Asa later recalls "a league between me and thee, and between my father and thy father" with Damascus, which suggests a treaty in Abijah's time.

people.text: Chronicles gives armies of 400,000 for Judah and 800,000 for Israel.

claim.text: Chronicles says Abijah's acts, ways and sayings are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.

first.text: Kings calls him Abijam.

second.text: Chronicles calls him Abijah.

first.text: Kings: "Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom".

second.text: Chronicles: "Michaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah"; elsewhere Chronicles calls Abijah's mother "Maachah the daughter of Absalom".

first.text: Kings: he walked in his father's sins, and there was war with Jeroboam. No battle is told.

second.text: Chronicles: no verdict, a speech for the LORD's covenant with David, and a great victory.

questions.question: Who was Abijah's mother: Maachah daughter of Abishalom, or Michaiah daughter of Uriel?

views.label: Two names for one woman
views.holders: Kimchi and Rashi (as reported in the Pulpit Commentary, 1881); John Gill (1748–63); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871)

argument.text: She had two names, perhaps taking a new one when she became queen; the names are too unlike for a copying slip.

views.label: One woman, granddaughter of Absalom
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); J. R. Lumby (1886); Ellicott's commentary

argument.text: "Daughter" means granddaughter: Absalom's daughter Tamar married Uriel of Gibeah, and "Michaiah" is a copyist's slip for Maachah, which the Greek, Syriac and Arabic versions read.
She might be the natural daughter of one man and the adopted daughter, or granddaughter, of the other; or Uriel and Absalom were one man.

views.label: Two Maachahs confused
views.holders: E. Bertheau, after O. Thenius (as reported, and rejected, by C. F. Keil, 1872)

argument.text: Abijah's mother and Asa's mother were different women whom the text has run together.

notSaid: Scripture does not give Abijah's age when he began to reign.

Scripture does not say how Abijah died; both books say only that he slept with his fathers.

claim.text: "In his days the land was quiet ten years."
He put away the sodomites and the idols his fathers had made, and took away the altars of strange gods.
While the land had rest he built fenced cities with walls, towers, gates and bars.
Zerah came with "a thousand thousand" and 300 chariots to Mareshah. Asa cried to the LORD, and the Ethiopians fled as far as Gerar.
After Azariah son of Oded's message, Judah, Benjamin and people from the north gathered in the third month of his fifteenth year and swore a covenant to seek the LORD.
He removed Maachah from being queen because of her idol in a grove, and burnt the idol by the brook Kidron.
Baasha built Ramah to cut Judah off. Chronicles dates it to Asa's thirty-sixth year.
Asa sent the temple and palace silver and gold to Ben-hadad of Damascus, who broke his league with Baasha and struck northern Israel. Asa used Ramah's stones to build Geba and Mizpah.
Hanani the seer rebuked him for relying on Syria; Asa put him in prison.
In his thirty-ninth year his feet were diseased, "until his disease was exceeding great".
He died in his forty-first year and was laid on a bed of spices, with "a very great burning" for him.

worship.text: Idols and the sodomites removed; the queen mother's idol burnt.
A covenant to seek the LORD, with death for whoever would not (Chronicles).
Yet the high places were not removed.

building.text: Fenced cities in Judah (Chronicles), and Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah built with Ramah's stones.

alliances.text: A league with Ben-hadad of Damascus, bought with the temple treasures.

people.text: Chronicles gives an army of 300,000 from Judah and 280,000 from Benjamin.
People from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon came over to him "in abundance".

claim.text: The Spirit of God came on him, and he told Asa "The LORD is with you, while ye be with him"; Asa took courage and put away the idols.

quote.text: The LORD is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.

claim.text: He rebuked Asa for relying on the king of Syria, and was put in prison for it.

quote.text: Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars.

claim.text: Ben-hadad took Asa's gift and attacked Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maachah and Naphtali.
Zerah's army came against Judah with Lubims among them, and was defeated at Mareshah.

first.text: Kings has Baasha die and Elah succeed in Asa's twenty-sixth year.

second.text: Chronicles dates Baasha's building of Ramah to Asa's thirty-sixth year.

first.text: Kings: "there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days".

second.text: Chronicles: "there was no more war unto the five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa".

first.text: Kings: "the high places were not removed".

second.text: Chronicles says both that he "took away … the high places" and that "the high places were not taken away out of Israel".

first.text: Kings says only that in old age he was diseased in his feet.

second.text: Chronicles adds Hanani's rebuke and prison, the date of the disease, his turning to physicians, and his burial with spices.

first.text: Kings has no Zerah, no Azariah son of Oded and no covenant.

second.text: Chronicles tells all three.

questions.question: Was Maachah Asa's mother or his grandmother?

argument.text: She is called his mother "not because she brought him forth, but because she brought him up".

views.label: Grandmother who kept the queen mother's office

argument.text: Abijam's mother Maachah stayed queen mother into Asa's reign, perhaps because Asa's own mother died early, until he deposed her.

views.label: Hard to solve; perhaps the grandmother kept her place
views.holders: Pulpit Commentary (1881), after K. Bähr's doubt

argument.text: Bähr doubted that the Hebrew word for mother can mean grandmother here. The note grants that the difficulty "by no means admits of a ready solution", but suggests the best explanation is that the grandmother kept her position, perhaps because Asa's own mother was dead.

questions.question: How can Baasha attack in Asa's thirty-sixth year, when Kings has him dead in Asa's twenty-sixth?

views.label: Counted from the division of the kingdom
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–85); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); in part W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: The thirty-sixth year is counted from the split of the kingdom, which equals Asa's sixteenth year. Ellicott called this idea "absurd", and Keil held the Hebrew cannot mean it.

views.label: A copyist changed the numeral
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); Joseph Benson (1811–18); Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Similar Hebrew numeral letters were confused. Keil reads the fifteenth and sixteenth years (30 for 10); Benson and the Pulpit Commentary read the twenty-sixth.

views.label: A different reckoning in the Chronicler's source

argument.text: Either the Chronicler followed a different calculation found in one of his documents, or the text is unsound.

questions.question: "War … all their days" or "no more war unto the five and thirtieth year"?

argument.text: Kings means a standing hostility with raids; Chronicles means open, declared war.
The Chronicler modified the older text to give a date for the outbreak of active fighting.

views.label: Only a broad reading reconciles them

argument.text: Nothing serious happened until the war with Baasha had gone on for several years.

questions.question: Did Asa and Jehoshaphat remove the high places or not?

views.label: Two kinds of high place
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–85); John Gill (1748–63); J. R. Lumby (1886)

argument.text: They removed the high places used for idols but left those where the LORD was worshipped unlawfully.

views.label: The kings tried, the people did not follow

argument.text: The kings abolished them but could not carry the reform through in the nation. Keil rejects the two-kinds view.

views.label: Removed in Judah, not in Israel

argument.text: Chronicles says he took them away "out of all the cities of Judah" but not "out of Israel".
The Chronicler incorporates traditions that contradict each other; if the removal happened, it had only partial success.

notSaid: Scripture does not give Asa's age when he began to reign.
Scripture does not name Asa's disease beyond its being "in his feet".
Scripture does not say who Zerah the Ethiopian served or where he came from beyond "Ethiopians and Lubims".

rulers.title: King of Judah

verdict.text: doing that which was right in the eyes of the LORD

comparison.text: And he walked in all the ways of Asa his father; he turned not aside from it

claim.text: He placed forces in the fenced cities of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa had taken.
In his third year he sent princes, Levites and priests through the cities of Judah with "the book of the law of the LORD".
Philistines brought presents and tribute silver; Arabians brought 7,700 rams and 7,700 he goats.
He "joined affinity with Ahab"; his son Jehoram married Ahab's daughter.
He went with Ahab against Ramoth-gilead after Micaiah warned of defeat. Mistaken for the king of Israel, he cried out and the chariots turned away; Ahab was killed.
He set judges in every fenced city and a court in Jerusalem of Levites, priests and heads of families, saying "ye judge not for man, but for the LORD".

events.label: Against Moab with Jehoram of Israel

claim.text: He joined Jehoram of Israel and the king of Edom against Mesha of Moab. Out of water, they asked Elisha, who spoke only out of regard for Jehoshaphat.
His ships of Tharshish, built to go to Ophir for gold, were wrecked at Ezion-geber.

Chronicles: he "sought not unto Baalim" and his heart "was lifted up in the ways of the LORD".
He brought people back to the LORD from Beersheba to mount Ephraim.

building.text: Castles and store cities in Judah (Chronicles).
Ships at Ezion-geber that never sailed.

alliances.text: "Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel."
Allied with Ahab at Ramoth-gilead and with Jehoram of Israel against Moab, saying to each "I am as thou art".
Edom had "no king … a deputy was king" in his time.

people.text: Chronicles lists over a million fighting men under five commanders.
"The fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms" round about, so they made no war on him (Chronicles).

claim.text: When Jehoshaphat asked for "a prophet of the LORD besides", Micaiah was brought and foretold Israel scattered and Ahab's death.
He met Jehoshaphat on his return from Ramoth-gilead with rebuke and praise; Chronicles cites his book as the record of the reign.

claim.text: He killed his six brothers, to whom Jehoshaphat had given fenced cities, and some princes of Israel.
Edom made its own king. Jehoram crossed to Zair by night and struck the Edomites around him, but Edom stayed free "unto this day".
Libnah revolted at the same time.
He made high places in the mountains of Judah and led Jerusalem astray.
A writing came from Elijah the prophet foretelling a great plague on his people and house and a disease of his bowels.
They carried off the king's goods, wives and sons, all but the youngest, Jehoahaz.

He made high places in the mountains of Judah (Chronicles).

alliances.text: He married "the daughter of Ahab", tying Judah's throne to the house of Omri.

people.text: Edom and Libnah broke away from Judah.
Philistines and Arabians broke into Judah and took the royal household (Chronicles).

claim.text: Chronicles alone tells that "a writing" came to Jehoram from Elijah the prophet.

quote.text: And thou shalt have great sickness by disease of thy bowels, until thy bowels fall out by reason of the sickness day by day.

claim.text: His wife was Ahab's daughter, and Ahab's son Jehoram reigned in Samaria at the same time.

first.text: Kings: he "slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in the city of David".

second.text: Chronicles: an incurable disease, no burning, buried in the city of David "but not in the sepulchres of the kings".

first.text: Kings names only Ahaziah as his son and successor.

second.text: Chronicles: raiders took all his sons "save Jehoahaz, the youngest".

first.text: Kings has no murder of his brothers, no Elijah letter, no raid and no disease.

second.text: Chronicles tells all four.

questions.question: When did Jehoram begin? Kings dates Joram of Israel's accession both to "the second year of Jehoram" of Judah and to "the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat", and Jehoram's own to Joram's fifth year, "Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah".

views.label: A viceroy and then a consort before reigning alone

argument.text: Ussher made Jehoram viceroy in 898 BC and his father's consort in 892, reigning alone from 889.

views.label: A co-regency with Jehoshaphat from 854 BC
views.holders: L. McFall (1991), revising E. R. Thiele

argument.text: 2 Kgs 1:17 counts from Jehoram's co-regency (from September 854); 2 Kgs 8:16 marks his sole reign from 848; the phrase "Jehoshaphat being then king" need not be cut from the text.

questions.question: How could Elijah write to Jehoram, when Kings tells Elijah's departure before Jehoram's reign?

views.label: Written beforehand and delivered later
views.holders: Kimchi (as reported by John Gill, 1748–63); Matthew Poole (1683–85)

argument.text: Elijah foresaw Jehoram's sins and left the writing, perhaps with Elisha, to be delivered in due time.

views.label: A copyist wrote Elijah for Elisha
views.holders: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); Joseph Benson (1811–18); W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: The name was originally Elisha, who was active in Jehoshaphat's day.
The date of Elijah's departure cannot be fixed; Kings tells it out of time order, and Elijah may have lived into Jehoram's reign.

views.label: A later writer's composition
views.holders: E. Bertheau (as reported, and rejected, by C. F. Keil, 1872); W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: The letter in its present form comes from a later historian, or adapts Elijah's words to Jehoram's case.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Jehoram's mother. He is one of only two kings of Judah whose mother Kings leaves out; the other is Ahaz.
Kings does not name Jehoram's wife at this point; it calls her "the daughter of Ahab". Her name, Athaliah, comes with her son's record.
Scripture does not say when Elijah wrote the letter.

rulers.name: Ahaziah
rulers.title: King of Judah
rulers.tagline: One year in Jerusalem, killed in Jehu's revolt.

identifications.text: Chronicles also calls him Jehoahaz (as Jehoram's youngest son) and, once, Azariah. He is not Ahaziah son of Ahab, king of Israel.

synchronism.text: In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel did Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah begin to reign.

mother.name: Athaliah, the daughter of Omri king of Israel

verdict.text: and did evil in the sight of the LORD, as did the house of Ahab

burial.text: buried him in his sepulchre with his fathers in the city of David

verdict.text: Wherefore he did evil in the sight of the LORD like the house of Ahab

comparison.text: He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab: for his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly.

burial.text: when they had slain him, they buried him

reign.text: One year (2 Kgs 8:26; 2 Chr 22:2). His age is twenty-two in Kings and forty-two in Chronicles.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers

accession.text: Chronicles says the people of Jerusalem made him king because raiders had killed all his older brothers.

quote.text: In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel did Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah begin to reign.
And in the eleventh year of Joram the son of Ahab began Ahaziah to reign over Judah.

claim.text: He went with Joram of Israel against Hazael of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, where Joram was wounded.
He went down to Jezreel to see the wounded Joram.
Jehu killed Joram at Naboth's field. Ahaziah fled and was struck down on the way.
Jehu killed forty-two men who said "We are the brethren of Ahaziah" on their way to visit the royal children; Chronicles calls them princes of Judah and sons of Ahaziah's brothers.

worship.text: He walked in the way of the house of Ahab, "for he was the son in law of the house of Ahab".

alliances.text: He fought beside Joram of Israel against Hazael of Syria.

people.text: Chronicles: after his death "the house of Ahaziah had no power to keep still the kingdom".

claim.text: Hazael king of Syria fought Israel and Judah at Ramoth-gilead.
Ahaziah died in the same revolt that ended Ahab's line in Israel.

A broken Aramaic victory stone from Tel Dan, found in 1993–94. Its speaker, generally taken to be Hazael of Damascus, claims to have killed a king of Israel and a king of "the house of David". Both names are broken; Biran and Naveh restored them as Joram son of Ahab and Ahaziah son of Jehoram. Kings gives the killing of both kings to Jehu.

first.text: Kings: "Two and twenty years old was Ahaziah when he began to reign".

second.text: Chronicles: "Forty and two years old was Ahaziah when he began to reign"; his father had died at forty.

first.text: Kings: struck by Ibleam, he fled to Megiddo and died there; his servants carried him to Jerusalem.

second.text: Chronicles: hidden in Samaria, he was caught, brought to Jehu and slain; they buried him.

first.text: Kings gives the twelfth year of Joram in one place and the eleventh in another.

second.text: Chronicles gives no cross-date.

questions.question: Was Ahaziah twenty-two or forty-two when he began to reign?

views.label: Two reckonings: co-king and sole king
views.holders: Geneva Bible notes (1599); Kimchi and Abarbanel (as reported by John Gill, 1748–63)

argument.text: He was made king at twenty-two while his father lived, and confirmed at forty-two. John Gill rejected this as received "without any proof".

views.label: Forty-two years of his mother's dynasty
views.holders: John Lightfoot (as reported by Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, 1871); Matthew Poole (1683–85)

argument.text: Forty-two counts the years of the house of Omri, not his age.

views.label: A copyist confused two numeral letters
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); J. R. Lumby (1887); John Gill; Pulpit Commentary (1881)

argument.text: The Hebrew letters for 20 and 40 were confused; forty-two is impossible, since his father died at forty.

questions.question: Did Ahaziah die at Megiddo or in Samaria?

argument.text: Chronicles means the territory of Samaria, which included Megiddo.

views.label: Too brief to reconcile with certainty

argument.text: Keil offers two orders of events but says the accounts are too short to settle it.

views.label: Two traditions; Kings more exact
views.holders: C. J. Ellicott's commentary; W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: Kings names definite places and is the more trustworthy; forced combinations are to be avoided. Ellicott adds that such differences show the two accounts are independent.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Ahaziah's wife here; Zibiah of Beersheba is named later as the mother of his son Joash.
No prophet is said to have spoken to Ahaziah himself.

rulers.name: Athaliah
rulers.title: Queen who reigned over Judah
rulers.tagline: Six years on David's throne, the only woman to reign over Judah.

identifications.text: Kings and Chronicles call her "the daughter of Omri" and say Jehoram's wife was "the daughter of Ahab". The text does not name her mother; the site's family data links her to Ahab and Jezebel.

reign.text: Six years, while the boy Joash was hidden in the temple (2 Kgs 11:3; 2 Chr 22:12). Scripture gives her no regnal formula: no cross-date, age, verdict, source note or burial.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: 6 years (2 Kgs 11:3). Scripture gives lengths and cross-dates, never BC years.

scriptureSays.text: "Athaliah did reign over the land." That one sentence (in Chronicles, "Athaliah reigned over the land") is all either book says about her rule itself; the rest tells how it began and how it ended.
As queen mother she was her son Ahaziah's counsellor "to do wickedly".
Chronicles later calls her "that wicked woman" and says her sons broke up the house of God and gave its dedicated things to the Baalim.
Neither book gives her any part of the formula it gives the kings: no verdict, mother's name, age, stated length, source note or burial. The six years are known from the time Joash was hidden.

accession.text: When her son Ahaziah died in Jehu's revolt she "arose and destroyed all the seed royal".
Jehosheba, King Joram's daughter and Ahaziah's sister, hid the infant Joash and his nurse in a bedchamber; Chronicles adds she was the wife of Jehoiada the priest.

claim.text: She killed the royal heirs, all but the hidden infant Joash.
Joash was hidden with Jehosheba in the house of the LORD six years.
In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest made a covenant with the captains and guard (Chronicles: Levites and heads of families) and showed them the king's son.
They crowned Joash, gave him "the testimony", anointed him and cried "God save the king".

Hearing the noise she came into the temple, rent her clothes and cried "Treason, Treason". Jehoiada had her taken out and killed at the horse entrance to the king's house, not in the house of the LORD.

events.label: The house of Baal broken down

claim.text: The people broke down the house of Baal and killed Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars.

worship.text: At her fall there was a house of Baal in Jerusalem with its own priest, Mattan.
Chronicles: her sons broke up the house of God and gave its dedicated things to the Baalim.

people.text: At Joash's crowning "all the people of the land rejoiced", and after her death "the city was in quiet".

claim.text: Jehu, who killed her son and her family in Israel, reigned in Samaria; Joash began in Jehu's seventh year.

first.text: Kings: Jehoiada brought in the rulers over hundreds, "the captains and the guard".

second.text: Chronicles: the Levites and priests gathered from all Judah kept the king; only priests and Levites entered the house.

first.text: Kings names her Jehosheba, daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah.

second.text: Chronicles names her Jehoshabeath and adds that she was the wife of Jehoiada the priest.

notSaid: Scripture gives Athaliah no regnal formula: no cross-date to Israel, no age, no verdict formula, no source note and no burial.
Scripture does not say how old she was or how her six years were governed.
Scripture does not name Jezebel as her mother.
Scripture does not say she built the house of Baal; it says the house and its priest were there when she fell.

rulers.name: Joash
rulers.title: King of Judah
rulers.tagline: Forty years in Jerusalem, crowned at seven.

identifications.text: Kings calls him both Jehoash and Joash. He is not Jehoash (Joash) son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel in Amaziah's day.

synchronism.text: In the seventh year of Jehu Jehoash began to reign

verdict.text: And Jehoash did that which was right in the sight of the LORD all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him.

death.text: His servants Jozachar and Jehozabad conspired and killed him in the house of Millo.

burial.text: they buried him with his fathers in the city of David

sourcesCited.text: are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?

burial.text: they buried him in the city of David, but they buried him not in the sepulchres of the kings

sourcesCited.text: they are written in the story of the book of the kings

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: 40 years (2 Kgs 12:1). Scripture gives lengths and cross-dates, never BC years.

verdictNotes.text: Both books limit the verdict to part of his reign: right "all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him" (Kings), "all the days of Jehoiada the priest" (Chronicles). That is why this page marks it as mixed.
But also: "the high places were not taken away".
Chronicles adds that after Jehoiada died the princes turned to groves and idols, and the king had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in the temple court.

accession.text: Hidden six years in the temple, he was brought out in the seventh year by Jehoiada the priest, crowned and anointed, and set on the throne.
Jehoiada made a covenant "between the LORD and the king and the people".

quote.text: In the seventh year of Jehu Jehoash began to reign
In the three and twentieth year of Joash the son of Ahaziah king of Judah Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria

A chest with a hole in the lid collected the money; carpenters, masons and builders repaired the temple.
Jehoiada died at 130 and was buried among the kings "because he had done good in Israel".
Zechariah son of Jehoiada rebuked the people; they stoned him "at the commandment of the king" in the temple court.
Hazael of Syria took Gath and turned toward Jerusalem; Joash sent him the hallowed things and gold of temple and palace, and he went away.
At the end of the year a small Syrian army defeated a great host of Judah and killed the princes.
His servants conspired and killed him.

Yet "the people still sacrificed and burnt incense in the high places".
After Jehoiada's death Judah "served groves and idols" (Chronicles).

Chronicles: vessels of gold and silver made from the money left over.

alliances.text: Tribute to Hazael of Syria from the temple and palace treasures.

people.text: "All the princes and all the people rejoiced" to give to the chest (Chronicles).

quote.text: Why transgress ye the commandments of the LORD, that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you.

claim.text: "Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again unto the LORD … but they would not give ear."
Hazael took Gath and threatened Jerusalem.

first.text: Kings: the priests had failed by his twenty-third year; Jehoiada set a chest beside the altar; no vessels were made from the money.

second.text: Chronicles: the Levites were slow; the chest stood at the gate for the tax Moses laid on Israel; vessels were made from what was left.

first.text: Kings: Joash bought Hazael off with the treasures.

second.text: Chronicles: a small Syrian army defeated Judah and "executed judgment against Joash".

first.text: Kings: a conspiracy by Jozachar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer, no reason given; buried with his fathers in the city of David.

second.text: Chronicles: Zabad son of Shimeath an Ammonitess and Jehozabad son of Shimrith a Moabitess, "for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada"; not buried in the kings' tombs.

first.text: Kings has nothing of Jehoiada's death, the idolatry after it, or Zechariah.

second.text: Chronicles tells all three.

questions.question: Is the Zechariah of 2 Chronicles 24 the "Zacharias son of Barachias" of Matthew 23:35?

views.label: Yes; Jehoiada had a second name, or was the grandfather
views.holders: Geneva Bible notes (1599); Pulpit Commentary on Chronicles

argument.text: Jehoiada was also called Barachiah, or Zechariah was Jehoiada's grandson. Ellicott called these hypotheses invented "without a shadow of evidence".

views.label: Yes; "son of Barachias" is a slip or an addition
views.holders: A. Carr (1878); Ellicott's commentary (Plumptre); H. A. W. Meyer (1879); A. B. Bruce (1897)

argument.text: Abel to Zechariah spans the Hebrew canon, Genesis to Chronicles; the father's name, absent in Luke 11:51, came from confusion with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah.

views.label: No; another Zacharias
views.holders: Reported by A. Carr (1878) and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew (1892)

argument.text: Some took it as a prophecy of the Zacharias son of Baruch killed in the temple in AD 67–68 (Josephus); Origen reported a tradition that it was John the Baptist's father. Carr thought the first "hardly probable".

notSaid: Kings does not say why his servants killed him.
Scripture does not say how old Jehoiada was when Joash was crowned.

burial.text: buried him with his fathers in the city of Judah

sourcesCited.text: are they not written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel?

dates.label: Scripture's numbers

events.label: Edom defeated in the Valley of Salt

claim.text: He killed 10,000 of Edom in the valley of salt and took Selah, naming it Joktheel.
The sent-home Israelite soldiers fell on Judah's cities from Samaria to Beth-horon and killed 3,000.
He set up the gods of Seir as his gods and burned incense to them.
He challenged Jehoash, who answered with the parable of the thistle and the cedar.
Judah was beaten; Jehoash captured Amaziah, broke down 400 cubits of Jerusalem's wall and took the treasures and hostages.

worship.text: The people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.
Edom's gods worshipped by the king (Chronicles).

alliances.text: Israelite mercenaries hired and dismissed (Chronicles).

people.text: Jerusalem's wall breached and hostages taken to Samaria.

claim.text: He told Amaziah to send the Israelite army home: "the LORD is not with Israel".

quote.text: The LORD is able to give thee much more than this.

claim.text: Sent because Amaziah sought Edom's gods; the king cut him off, and he said God had determined to destroy him.

quote.text: Why hast thou sought after the gods of the people, which could not deliver their own people out of thine hand?

claim.text: Jehoash of Israel defeated and captured him; Jeroboam II began in Amaziah's fifteenth year.

first.text: Kings: Jehoash tells him "thine heart hath lifted thee up"; "Amaziah would not hear".

second.text: Chronicles: "it came of God … because they sought after the gods of Edom".

first.text: Kings: "at Jerusalem with his fathers in the city of David".

second.text: Chronicles: "with his fathers in the city of Judah".

first.text: Kings tells the Edom campaign in one verse.

second.text: Chronicles adds the muster, the hired army, the man of God, the 10,000 thrown from the rock, the raid on Judah, Edom's gods and the prophet's rebuke.

questions.question: Why does only Chronicles tell of Amaziah's Edomite gods and hired army?

argument.text: Chronicles supplements Kings from independent sources, and these details explain the later war with Israel.

views.label: A principle applied to history
views.holders: E. Bertheau and O. Thenius (as reported by C. F. Keil and Ellicott, who reject it)

argument.text: The idolatry was inferred from Amaziah's defeat rather than drawn from a record.

views.label: A known ancient policy
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); W. E. Barnes (1899)

notSaid: Scripture does not say whether Amaziah was released by Jehoash or how long he was held.

synchronism.text: In the twenty and seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel began Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah to reign.

burial.text: they buried him with his fathers in the city of David

sourcesCited.text: are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?

verdict.text: And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Amaziah did.

burial.text: they buried him with his fathers in the field of the burial which belonged to the kings; for they said, He is a leper

Chronicles: "as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper" — then "his heart was lifted up to his destruction".

verdict.text: And he did that which was evil in the eyes of the LORD, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.

death.text: Jeremiah 52 adds that the king of Babylon "put him in prison till the day of his death".

reign.text: Eleven years, from the age of twenty-one (2 Kgs 24:18; 2 Chr 36:11; Jer 52:1).

dates.label: Scripture's numbers

verdictNotes.text: Chronicles: he rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, "who had made him swear by God", and "stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart".
Kings: "through the anger of the LORD" Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

accession.text: Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah king after taking Jehoiachin, and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Ezekiel: the king of Babylon "hath taken of the king's seed, and made a covenant with him, and hath taken an oath of him".

quote.text: in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar
which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon

claim.text: Messengers from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon came to Zedekiah in Jerusalem; Jeremiah sent them yokes.
In his fourth year the prophet Hananiah broke Jeremiah's yoke and promised the exiles' return within two years.
Seraiah went with Zedekiah into Babylon in the fourth year of his reign.
He rebelled against the king of Babylon, sending ambassadors to Egypt for horses and men.
On the tenth day of the tenth month of his ninth year Nebuchadnezzar camped against Jerusalem and built forts round it.
He made a covenant to free Hebrew slaves; the people later forced them back into service.
When Pharaoh's army came out of Egypt the Chaldeans lifted the siege; Jeremiah said they would return and burn the city.
Jeremiah was held in the court of the prison in the tenth year and put in a miry dungeon; the king asked him secretly for a word from the LORD.
On the ninth day of the fourth month of his eleventh year, with famine in the city, the wall was broken and the men of war fled by night.
The Chaldeans overtook him in the plains of Jericho; at Riblah his sons were killed before his eyes and his eyes put out.
Nebuzar-adan burned the house of the LORD, the king's house and all Jerusalem, and broke down its walls.
Nebuchadnezzar set Gedaliah over the people left in the land.

worship.text: "All the chief of the priests, and the people, transgressed very much" and polluted the temple (Chronicles).
They mocked the LORD's messengers "till there was no remedy".

alliances.text: Sworn to Nebuchadnezzar; turned to Egypt.

people.text: The people left were carried away, except the poor of the land left as vinedressers and husbandmen.
Chronicles: the land kept its sabbaths seventy years, until the first year of Cyrus.

claim.text: He told Zedekiah to surrender to Babylon's princes and live; he was imprisoned, yet the king consulted him in secret.

quote.text: If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon’s princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire

claim.text: In Babylon he foretold that the prince would be taken in the LORD's net and brought to Babylon, "yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there".

quote.text: and I will bring him to Babylon to the land of the Chaldeans; yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there

claim.text: He broke Jeremiah's yoke and promised peace within two years; Jeremiah said he made the people trust in a lie.
Nebuchadnezzar made him king, besieged him and judged him at Riblah; his captain Nebuzar-adan burned Jerusalem in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year.
Pharaoh's army came out of Egypt during the siege and went back.

After taking Jerusalem in 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar "appointed a king of his own choice" there; scholars take him to be Mattaniah-Zedekiah. The chronicle stops in 594 BC, so it does not cover the destruction of Jerusalem.

Hebrew letters on potsherds found in 1935 in the gate of Lachish. In letter 4 an officer says his post is watching for the signals of Lachish, because they cannot see Azekah — compare Jeremiah 34:7, where Lachish and Azekah are the last fortified cities standing. Letter 3 mentions "the prophet". No king is named.

first.text: Kings: Mattaniah was Jehoiachin's "father's brother".

second.text: Chronicles: Nebuchadnezzar made "Zedekiah his brother king".

first.text: Kings: "in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month".

second.text: Jeremiah: "in the fifth month, in the tenth day of the month".

first.text: Kings tells the siege, the flight, Riblah and the burning in detail.

second.text: Chronicles tells no siege or flight; it gives the people's sins, the seventy years, and Cyrus's decree.

questions.question: Did Jerusalem fall in 587 or 586 BC?

argument.text: McFall keeps Thiele's date: the city fell on 9 Tammuz, 18 July 586.

views.label: 587 BC
views.holders: W. F. Albright (1945); R. C. Young (2005)

argument.text: Albright put the storming in August 587; Young dates 9 Tammuz to 587.

questions.question: Was Zedekiah Jehoiachin's brother or his uncle?

views.label: "Brother" in the wide sense of kinsman

argument.text: The word is used loosely for a blood relation; he was in fact Jehoiachin's father's brother.

views.label: Kings is the more accurate
views.holders: J. R. Lumby (1887); W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: Chronicles is wrong unless the word means "kinsman".

views.label: The Chronicler's copy was damaged
views.holders: O. Thenius (as reported by Ellicott's commentary)

argument.text: The word for uncle had become illegible in the manuscript the Chronicler used.

questions.question: Was the temple burned on the seventh or the tenth day of the fifth month?

views.label: The fire lasted from the seventh to the tenth
views.holders: Geneva Bible notes (1599); Matthew Poole (1683–85), as one option

argument.text: He arrived on the seventh and burned the temple on the tenth, or the fire burned for three days.

views.label: He set out on the seventh and arrived on the tenth
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–85); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871)

argument.text: Kings gives Nebuzar-adan's departure from Riblah, Jeremiah his arrival.

views.label: A copyist confused the numerals; which is right cannot be known
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); A. W. Streane (1881)

argument.text: The Hebrew letters for 7 and 10 were confused; the true day cannot now be decided.

views.label: A copyist's error; the tenth is right

argument.text: Seven was misread for ten.

notSaid: Kings and Chronicles do not say when Zedekiah died; Jeremiah says only that he was in prison "till the day of his death".
Scripture does not say Zedekiah saw Babylon; Ezekiel says he would not see it.
